questions.q: In a state-vector simulator, what does array index 6 represent for a 3-qubit system (using index = 4·q1 + 2·q2 + q3)?
options: A fixed probability value that never changes during the simulation
The amplitude of basis state |110⟩, since 6 in binary is 110
The number of gates applied so far
The sixth qubit in the system
questions.explain: Each array index's binary representation directly encodes a computational basis state. Index 6 = binary 110 = |110⟩ (q1=1, q2=1, q3=0), and the array value at that position is that basis state's amplitude.

questions.q: Why does a real simulator apply a single-qubit gate using the 'index-pairing' trick instead of building the full 2^n × 2^n matrix for an n-qubit system?
options: Because the full matrix approach gives a mathematically different (incorrect) answer
Because the full matrix is mostly zeros and wastes enormous memory for large n; index-pairing only ever touches the fixed small 2×2 gate and the existing state array
Because building a matrix is not possible in JavaScript
Because index-pairing is the only method that works for the Hadamard gate specifically
questions.explain: Both approaches are mathematically equivalent, but the full 2^n × 2^n matrix is overwhelmingly sparse and grows exponentially with n, while index-pairing needs only the 2×2 gate and the 2^n-element state array — no extra matrix at all.

questions.q: In the lesson's applySingleQubitGate function, what do i0 and i1 represent for a given mask bit?
options: The pair of array indices that are identical except for the targeted qubit's bit (i0 has it 0, i1 has it 1), whose amplitudes the 2×2 gate matrix combines
The first and last indices of the entire state array
The real and imaginary parts of a single amplitude
Two completely unrelated qubits in the system
questions.explain: i0 = i (the targeted qubit's bit is 0) and i1 = i | mask (that same index with the targeted bit flipped to 1). The gate's 2×2 matrix is applied to exactly this pair's two amplitudes, independent of what the other qubits' bits are.

questions.q: When H was applied to qubit 1 of the 3-qubit state |000⟩ and the function was actually run, the result was [0.7071, 0, 0, 0, 0.7071, 0, 0, 0]. What does this confirm?
options: Qubit 3 was flipped to |1⟩
All three qubits are now in superposition simultaneously
The state became (|000⟩+|100⟩)/√2 — qubit 1 is in superposition, while qubits 2 and 3 remain fixed at |0⟩ in every nonzero term, matching what H on one qubit should do to a 3-qubit basis state
The simulation failed because there should be exactly one nonzero amplitude
questions.explain: Nonzero amplitudes sit only at index 0 (|000⟩) and index 4 (|100⟩), i.e. only q1 varies between 0 and 1 across the nonzero terms — exactly the expected effect of applying H to a single spectator-surrounded qubit.

questions.q: After chaining H(q1) then CNOT(q1→q2) onto |000⟩ in the lesson's actual node run, the final state was [0.7071,0,0,0,0,0,0.7071,0]. Why is this result considered validated rather than just asserted?
options: Because the code compiled without throwing an error

Because it exactly reproduces the Chapter 3 Bell-state result (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2 on qubits 1–2, with qubit 3 as an untouched spectator — matching an answer already independently derived by hand matrix multiplication
Because the amplitudes are both positive numbers
Because it used exactly two gates
questions.explain: A simulator function's correctness is checked by confirming it reproduces results already known to be correct from independent computation — here, the amplitude pattern at index 0 and index 6 matches the earlier hand-verified Bell state, now with qubit 3 along for the ride unchanged.
